questions.category: Legal Framework & Appointment of Bank Auditors
questions.question:
Case Scenario 1:
Vardhman Bank Ltd. is a scheduled commercial banking company incorporated under the Companies Act, 2013, while Pragati Bank is a prominent Nationalised Bank established under the Banking Companies (Acquisition and Transfer of Undertakings) Act. During the financial year 2023-24, both banks initiated the process of appointing statutory auditors. Vardhman Bank Ltd. convened its Annual General Meeting (AGM) of shareholders and passed an ordinary resolution appointing M/s K. Sharma & Co. as its statutory central auditor, without seeking prior approval from the Reserve Bank of India (RBI), contending that shareholders are the supreme appointing authority under the Companies Act, 2013. Simultaneously, Pragati Bank (the Nationalised Bank) finalized the appointment of four CA firms as joint statutory central auditors through its Board of Directors (BOD), having duly secured prior approval from the RBI. The appointment letter issued to each joint central auditor set out the period of appointment, particulars of previous auditors, and scope of assignment, but completely omitted the particulars of other joint central auditors and the statement of division of work. Meanwhile, for its branch audits, Pragati Bank engaged single CA firms as statutory branch auditors. One of the newly appointed branch auditors, CA Nitin, insisted that his appointment letter must also contain a statement of division of work and particulars of other branch auditors, similar to statutory central auditors.

Regarding the validity of the appointment of statutory central auditors by Vardhman Bank Ltd. and Pragati Bank under the relevant statutory provisions, which of the following statements is legally correct?
options: The appointment made by Vardhman Bank Ltd. is valid because under Section 139 of the Companies Act, 2013, the shareholders at an AGM possess unfettered authority to appoint statutory auditors without regulatory interference.

The appointment made by Vardhman Bank Ltd. is invalid in law because, for a banking company, approval of the Reserve Bank of India is mandatory before the appointment is made at the AGM of shareholders.
The appointment made by Pragati Bank through its Board of Directors is invalid because nationalised banks must also obtain shareholders' ratification at an AGM in addition to RBI approval.
Both appointments are void ab initio because statutory central auditors of all banking entities can only be appointed directly by the Comptroller and Auditor General of India (CAG).
questions.explanation: As per the legal framework governing banks, the appointing authority for a banking company is the AGM of shareholders, whereas for a nationalised bank, it is the bank acting through its Board of Directors. However, in either case, the prior approval of the Reserve Bank of India (RBI) is strictly required before the appointment is made. Since Vardhman Bank Ltd. appointed M/s K. Sharma & Co. at its AGM without obtaining prior RBI approval, the appointment is invalid in law. Pragati Bank, on the other hand, acted validly through its Board of Directors with prior approval of the RBI as required for nationalised banks.

questions.category: Legal Framework & Appointment of Bank Auditors
questions.question:
Principal enactments govern the functioning of various categories of banks in India. Which of the following correctly pairs the category of bank with its governing principal statutory enactment as specified in the legal framework?

1. Banking Company - Banking Regulation Act, 1949 and Companies Act, 2013
2. State Bank of India - State Bank of India Act, 1955
3. Central Bank & Overall Monetary Authority - Reserve Bank of India Act, 1934

Select the correct combination:
options: 1 and 2 only
2 and 3 only
1 and 3 only
1, 2 and 3
questions.explanation: The legal framework governing the functioning of banks in India comprises principal enactments including the Banking Regulation Act, 1949, the State Bank of India Act, 1955, the Reserve Bank of India Act, 1934, and the Companies Act, 2013. Banking companies are governed by both the Banking Regulation Act, 1949 and the Companies Act, 2013. State Bank of India is governed by the State Bank of India Act, 1955 alongside the Banking Regulation Act and RBI Act. All three statements accurately reflect the principal statutory enactments governing the banking sector in India.

questions.category: Special Considerations in Audit of Banks
questions.question:
Special audit considerations arise in the audit of banks due to several unique operating characteristics. Consider the following statements:

Statement I: Banking operations involve a particular nature of risks associated with transactions and significant exposures that can arise within a very short time.
Statement II: Banks operate with extensive dependence on information technology (IT) to process high volumes of transactions.
Statement III: Banking institutions operate in an environment heavily impacted by statutory and regulatory requirements and the continuing development of new services and banking practices.
Statement IV: Unlike commercial companies, banks are legally exempted from internal control oversight by Those Charged with Governance (TCWG).

Which of the above statements correctly describe peculiarities necessitating special audit considerations in banks?
options: Statements I, II and III only
Statements I, II and IV only
Statements II, III and IV only
Statements I, II, III and IV
questions.explanation: Special audit considerations arise in the audit of banks because of: (i) particular nature of risks associated with transactions, (ii) scale of banking operations and significant exposures which can arise within a short time, (iii) extensive dependence on IT to process transactions, (iv) effect of statutory and regulatory requirements, and (v) continuing development of new services and banking practices. Statement IV is false because oversight by Those Charged with Governance (TCWG) is an essential component of the bank's internal control and risk management process, and banks are never exempted from such governance oversight. Therefore, Statements I, II, and III are the only correct statements.

questions.category: Process of Conducting Audit of Banks
questions.question:
Match the stages of the banking audit process in Column I with their corresponding mandatory components in Column II:

Column I (Audit Stage)
A. Initial Considerations
B. Understanding
C. Risk Assessment
D. Execution

Column II (Components)
1. Engagement Team Discussions, Audit Materiality, Going Concern, Response to Assessed Risks
2. Identifying and Assessing ROMM, Risk of Fraud including Money Laundering, Specific Risks
3. Acceptance & Continuance, Declaration of Indebtedness, Terms of Engagement, Communication with Previous Auditor
4. Understanding Bank and Its Environment, Bank's Accounting Process, Risk Management Process (Oversight by TCWG, Control/Monitoring activities)

Select the correct match:
questions.explanation: As outlined in the banking audit process framework: Initial Considerations encompass acceptance & continuance, declaration of indebtedness, terms of audit engagements, communication with previous auditor, planning, and establishing the engagement team (A-3). Understanding includes understanding the bank and its environment including internal control, the accounting process, and the risk management process involving oversight by TCWG, identification/monitoring of risks, and control activities (B-4). Risk Assessment involves identifying and assessing ROMM, assessing risk of fraud including money laundering, and specific risks (C-2). Execution includes engagement team discussions, preparing response to assessed risks, determining audit materiality, and considering going concern (D-1).

questions.category: Special Considerations in IT Environment
questions.question:
During the statutory central audit of Apex Commercial Bank, the audit team requested detailed technical documentation from the Chief Information Officer (CIO) regarding the bank's IT architecture. The CIO declined to provide certain documents, asserting that auditors are only entitled to financial trial balances and that sharing IT interface mechanisms, exception report logic, and e-banking control designs violates bank cyber confidentiality.

In accordance with established audit guidance on Special Considerations in an IT Environment, which of the following areas is the bank IMPERATIVE to share with the statutory auditors?
options: Only the end-user login credentials and customer account passwords for testing security parameters.

Overall IT policy, data processing and data interface under various systems, process of generating disclosures, data integrity/security, controls on e-banking/internet products, and MIS/major exception reports along with their generation process.
Only the source code of the Core Banking Solution (CBS) and proprietary cryptographic keys used in automated teller machines (ATMs).
Only the hardware vendor purchase invoices and warranty certificates for mainframe servers.
questions.explanation: Considering the vital importance of IT systems in the preparation and presentation of financial statements, it is imperative that a bank shares detailed information with auditors. This includes: (i) Overall IT policy and structure of the bank's IT system, (ii) Data processing and data interface under various systems, (iii) Process of generating various information related to disclosures in FS, (iv) Data integrity and data security, (v) Controls on recording of various e-banking and internet banking products, and (vi) MIS reports and major exception reports and their process of generation. Refusal by bank management to furnish these areas impedes the auditor's ability to assess IT general controls and automated application controls.

questions.category: Special Considerations in IT Environment
questions.question: When undertaking an audit in a computerised bank, the auditor needs to evaluate key security control aspects within the IT infrastructure. Which of the following is NOT an essential security control aspect that the auditor must address as per the prescribed bank audit framework?
options: Ensuring that authorised, accurate and complete data is available for processing.
Ensuring that in case of power failure, the system restarts without distorting records.
Ensuring that the system automatically bypasses parameter change validations during high-volume end-of-day batch processing to avoid latency.
Verifying that segregation of duties is ensured while granting system access, parameter/user level changes are authenticated, and exceptional reports are authorised and verified daily.
questions.explanation: Key security control aspects that an auditor needs to address in a computerised bank include: (1) ensuring authorized, accurate, and complete data is available for processing; (2) ensuring that in case of power failure, the system restarts without distorting records; (3) ensuring the system prevents unauthorized amendments to programmes; (4) verifying segregation of duties while granting system access; (5) verifying that changes made in parameters or user levels are authenticated; and (6) verifying that exceptional reports are authorised and verified on a daily basis. Bypassing parameter change validations during batch processing is a severe control breakdown and directly contradicts security requirements that mandate strict authentication for all parameter changes. Therefore, this treatment strictly aligns with the regulatory framework prescribed by the Reserve Bank of India and applicable auditing standards. Candidates must ensure rigorous application of these statutory principles during banking and NBFC audit engagements.

questions.category: Internal Control in Selected Areas - Cash
questions.question:
Case Scenario 2:
During the statutory branch audit of Zenith Bank, MG Road Branch, the audit team examined the operational internal controls across several high-risk functional areas:
1. Cash Operations: Cash was held under the sole custody of the Chief Cashier to expedite morning counter opening. In addition, the Chief Cashier had been granted active system rights to post entries directly into customer ledger accounts and the Day Book. Physical cash was test-checked once a month by an external agency, and payments were released upon oral authorization from the Branch Manager.
2. Loans and Advances: The branch sanctioned an additional temporary overdraft limit of 35% over the existing sanctioned limit of a borrower for a period of 120 days to meet urgent operational expenses. Furthermore, credit facilities were disbursed prior to the execution of mortgage and hypothecation documents, and certain credit facilities had not been reviewed for over 15 months.
3. Inward Clearings: Cheques of Rs. 7,50,000 and Rs. 12,00,000 received in inward clearing were processed and credited without calling or emailing the drawer customers, as the branch manager claimed that calling customers was optional for amounts under Rs. 20,00,000.
4. Bills Purchased and Demand Drafts: At year-end, discount received on bills purchased having unexpired terms extending into the next financial year was credited 100% to the current year's profit and loss account. In respect of demand drafts issued by the branch, advice was sent to paying branches only upon monthly reconciliation rather than immediately.

Evaluate the internal controls observed in the Cash Operations of the branch against the established internal control benchmarks for banks. Which of the following evaluations is correct?
options: The cash controls are fully compliant because modern Core Banking Systems record electronic audit trails, making joint custody and restrictions on cashier posting rights redundant.

The cash controls display multiple severe deficiencies: cash must be kept in joint custody of two responsible officers, test-checked daily (in addition to normal checking by the chief cashier), the cashier should have no access to customer ledger accounts and Day Book, and payments must only be made after vouchers are passed by an authorised officer.
The only deficiency is the monthly test-check; cash custody by a single senior officer is permitted if covered by a banker's blanket insurance policy.
The cashier is permitted to post entries in customer ledgers provided high-value cash receipts are verified by an external auditor at the end of each quarter.
questions.explanation: Internal control guidelines for cash in banks strictly require that: (i) Cash should be kept in joint custody of two responsible officers, (ii) In addition to normal checking by the chief cashier, cash should be test-checked daily, (iii) The cashier should have NO access to customer ledger accounts and the Day Book, (iv) Payments should be made only after vouchers are passed by an authorised officer, and (v) High-value cash receipts and payments should be verified by a higher officer. The practices observed at Zenith Bank violate every single one of these fundamental internal controls. Therefore, this treatment strictly aligns with the regulatory framework prescribed by the Reserve Bank of India and applicable auditing standards. Candidates must ensure rigorous application of these statutory principles during banking and NBFC audit engagements.

2. In respect of demand drafts issued by the branch, advice was sent to paying branches only upon monthly reconciliation rather than immediately.

Regarding Inward Clearings, Bills Purchased, and Demand Drafts (DD) operations, which of the following conclusions represents the correct regulatory and accounting position?
options: For inward clearing cheques, RBI mandates calling or emailing the customer for cheques of Rs. 5 lakhs and above; discount received on unexpired bills purchased must be apportioned between two years (rebate on bills discounted); and all DDs issued must be immediately confirmed by advice to the paying branch.
The RBI threshold for calling customers on inward clearings is Rs. 10 lakhs; discount on bills purchased must be recognized entirely on cash receipt basis; and DD advices are optional.
Customer confirmation is only required for clearing cheques exceeding Rs. 50 lakhs; discount on bills is non-apportionable under AS 9; and DD advices are sent weekly.
Calling customers is a discretionary recommendation without mandatory standing; unexpired bill discount is treated as contingent liability; and DD confirmation can await monthly settlement.
questions.explanation: As per RBI guidelines, a branch is required to either call the customer or email him for any cheque received of Rs. 5 lakhs and above in respect of inward clearings. For bills purchased outstanding at the close of the year, discount received thereon relates partly to the unexpired period and must be properly apportioned between the two years (unexpired portion treated as Rebate on Bills Discounted). Furthermore, internal controls dictate that all Demand Drafts (DD) issued by a branch must be immediately confirmed by advice to the paying branch. Zenith Bank failed on all three counts.

questions.category: Internal Control in Selected Areas - Credit Card Operations
questions.question:
An effective internal control system over a bank's credit card operations must encompass specific surveillance and monitoring mechanisms. Which of the following procedures is NOT a designated internal control requirement for credit card operations as per bank audit guidelines?

1. Effective screening of applications and strict control over storage and issue of cards.
2. Prompt reporting by merchants of all settlements accepted through credit cards.
3. Ensuring statements are sent regularly and promptly to customers, with monitoring and follow-up of payments.
4. Delegating the authority to waive overdue credit card balances permanently to card-issuing sales executives without higher-level review.
options: 1 and 2 only
3 only
4 only
2 and 4 only
questions.explanation: Internal control systems for credit card operations require: (i) effective screening of applications, (ii) strict control over storage and issue of cards, (iii) prompt reporting by merchants of all settlements accepted through credit cards, (iv) ensuring statements are sent regularly and promptly to customers, (v) monitoring and follow-up of customer payments, (vi) identification of payments overdue beyond a reasonable period, and (vii) periodic review of credit card holders' accounts. Allowing sales executives to waive overdue balances without higher-level review (item 4) is an egregious control breakdown and is completely contrary to prudent risk management. Therefore, this treatment strictly aligns with the regulatory framework prescribed by the Reserve Bank of India and applicable auditing standards. Candidates must ensure rigorous application of these statutory principles during banking and NBFC audit engagements.

questions.category: Compliance with CRR and SLR Requirements
questions.question:
Case Scenario 3:
During the statutory audit of Shrestha Bank Ltd., the engagement team was tasked with auditing compliance with Cash Reserve Ratio (CRR) under Section 42 of the Reserve Bank of India Act, 1934 and Statutory Liquidity Ratio (SLR) under Section 24 of the Banking Regulation Act, 1949. The audit team selected 12 odd dates, all falling on alternate Fridays, to verify SLR compliance. While verifying the consolidation of Demand and Time Liabilities (DTL) prepared at Head Office from branch returns, the audit team observed the following accounting treatments:
1. Exclusions from Liabilities: The bank excluded from DTL computation: (a) Paid-up capital and reserves, (b) Loans taken from RBI, (c) Refinance taken from NABARD and SIDBI, (d) Margins held in sundry deposits for funded facilities, (e) Net income tax provision, and (f) Part amount of recoveries from borrowers in respect of bad debts.
2. Disputed Items: The management also excluded from DTL: (g) Cash collaterals received under collateralized derivative transactions, and (h) Net credit balance in branch adjustment accounts, arguing that these represent operational contra items.
3. Accrued Interest: The bank omitted interest accrued on deposits which had not yet been formally posted/accounted in the branch general ledgers from the DTL statement.

With respect to the selection of audit dates for verifying compliance with Statutory Liquidity Ratio (SLR) requirements, evaluate the audit team's procedure:
options: The audit team's procedure is fully compliant because alternate Fridays represent reporting reporting fortnights where SLR compliance is officially certified.
The audit team's procedure is defective because the audit guidelines explicitly mandate verifying compliance with SLR requirements on 12 odd dates not being Fridays.
The audit team should have selected the last day of each calendar month rather than 12 odd dates.
The audit team is only required to verify SLR on March 31st and September 30th as part of half-yearly reporting.
questions.explanation: Under the audit procedure for compliance with CRR and SLR requirements, the auditor is specifically required to 'Verify compliance with SLR requirements of 12 odd dates NOT being Fridays'. Selecting alternate Fridays is incorrect because banks already maintain and report fortnightly data on alternate Fridays; selecting 12 odd dates not being Fridays tests whether the bank maintains the required SLR on ongoing operational days throughout the year without dipping below statutory minimums. Therefore, this treatment strictly aligns with the regulatory framework prescribed by the Reserve Bank of India and applicable auditing standards. Candidates must ensure rigorous application of these statutory principles during banking and NBFC audit engagements.

Based on the prescribed DTL computation rules, evaluate the items excluded from liabilities by Shrestha Bank Ltd. under item (1):
- Paid up capital and reserves
- Loans taken from RBI and refinance from NABARD/SIDBI
- Margins held in sundry deposits for funded facilities
- Net income tax provision
- Part amount of recoveries from borrowers in respect of bad debts

Which of the following statements is correct?
options: All the items listed under item (1) are legitimately excluded from liabilities for DTL computation.
Paid-up capital and reserves must be included in DTL, but refinance from NABARD can be excluded.
Margins held in sundry deposits for funded facilities must be included in DTL; only non-funded facility margins are excluded.
Recoveries from borrowers in respect of bad debts must always be included in DTL as demand liabilities.

Thus, all items in (1) were correctly excluded. Therefore, this treatment strictly aligns with the regulatory framework prescribed by the Reserve Bank of India and applicable auditing standards. Regarding the disputed items (g - Cash collaterals under collateralized derivative transactions, h - Net credit balance in branch adjustment accounts) and the unposted accrued interest on deposits, what is the correct statutory treatment in DTL computation?
options: Management's exclusion of items (g) and (h) is correct, and interest accrued on deposits is includible only if already accounted in books.
Items (g) and (h), as well as interest accrued on deposits whether or not accounted in books of accounts, must be strictly INCLUDED in liabilities for DTL computation.

questions.category: Compliance with CRR and SLR Requirements

Which of the following items is correctly categorized as an INCLUSION in liabilities for the computation of Demand and Time Liabilities (DTL) of a bank?

1. Amount received from DICGC and ECGC
2. Amount received from court receiver and insurance companies for ad-hoc settlement
3. Adverse balances in nostro mirror account and borrowings from abroad
4. Unrealized gain/loss arising from derivatives transactions
options: 1 and 2
3 only
3 and 4
questions.explanation: Items 1, 2, and 4 (amounts received from DICGC/ECGC, amounts from court receiver/ad-hoc insurance claim settlements, and unrealized gain/loss arising from derivative transactions) are items specifically EXCLUDED from liabilities in DTL computation. questions.category: Asset Classification & Provisioning - Borrower-wise Classification
questions.question:
Case Scenario 4:
During the audit of Samriddhi Bank, Civil Lines Branch, the statutory branch auditor scrutinized the advances portfolio as of March 31, 2024. The following loan accounts were evaluated:
1. Borrower Alpha Pvt. Ltd.: Holds three distinct facilities with the branch - a Cash Credit facility of Rs. 80 lakhs (which is fully regular and serviced on time), a Term Loan of Rs. 50 lakhs (where interest and EMI installments have remained overdue for 110 days), and a Letter of Credit facility of Rs. 30 lakhs. The branch classified only the Term Loan as a Sub-Standard NPA while retaining the Cash Credit and LC facilities as Standard assets.
2. Borrower Beta Ltd.: Operating a working capital CC limit of Rs. 2 crores. The sanctioned limit expired on September 15, 2023, and had not been reviewed or renewed until March 31, 2024 (a lapse of 198 days). The latest stock statement available on record was dated October 20, 2023 (more than 5 months old). The branch treated the account as Standard, claiming that these are mere temporary deficiencies.
3. Borrower Gamma Corp.: The account was overdue for 120 days as of February 28, 2024. On March 29, 2024, the borrower deposited Rs. 15 lakhs, regularizing the entire overdue interest and principal. However, audit verification revealed that on March 30, 2024, the branch had sanctioned and disbursed a fresh clean personal loan of Rs. 18 lakhs to the promoter of Gamma Corp, which was utilized to fund the deposit.
4. Borrower Delta Infra: Advance covered by a Central Government guarantee overdue for 180 days. The bank has not invoked the guarantee.

Evaluate the branch's classification of Borrower Alpha Pvt. Ltd.'s facilities where only the irregular Term Loan was classified as NPA while the regular Cash Credit was kept as Standard:
options: The branch's action is correct because asset classification in banking is facility-wise, allowing performing credit lines to be retained as Standard.

The branch's action is incorrect because asset classification is borrower-wise and not facility-wise; all facilities granted by a bank to a borrower must be treated as NPA if any one facility becomes irregular.
The branch must classify the Cash Credit as Sub-Standard only if the aggregate exposure across all facilities exceeds Rs. 1 crore.
The branch is permitted to segregate facilities provided the Cash Credit is secured by primary hypothecation of current assets.
questions.explanation: As per RBI prudential norms, asset classification must be borrower-wise and not facility-wise. It is mandatory that if one facility granted to a borrower slips into the NPA category, all facilities granted by the bank to that borrower must be treated as NPA, and not just the particular facility which has become irregular. Therefore, because Alpha Pvt. Ltd.'s Term Loan is an NPA (overdue > 90 days), the Cash Credit and LC facilities must also be classified as NPA.

questions.category: Verification of Asset Classification - Drawing Power Calculation
questions.question:
In the calculation and verification of Drawing Power (DP) for working capital advances in banks, which of the following represents an accurate internal control and audit requirement?

1. Drawing power must be calculated strictly in accordance with guidelines formulated by the Board of Directors of the bank.
2. Special consideration should be given to proper reporting and deduction of sundry creditors and stocks covered under Letters of Credit (LCs)/guarantees to prevent double financing.
3. Drawing power needs to be calculated with special care in case of working capital advances to companies engaged in construction business.
4. Stock auditor's reports should be reviewed by the statutory auditor for comments made on drawing power.
options: 1 and 2 only
1, 2 and 3 only
2, 3 and 4 only
questions.explanation: Audit procedures for drawing power calculation require the auditor to: (i) Ensure that drawing power is calculated as per guidelines formulated by the BOD; (ii) Give special consideration to proper reporting of sundry creditors and stocks covered under LCs/guarantees for calculating DP (as these are unpaid stocks); (iii) Calculate DP carefully in case of working capital advances to companies engaged in construction business; and (iv) Review stock auditor's reports for comments made on drawing power and stock valuation. All four statements are correct. Therefore, this treatment strictly aligns with the regulatory framework prescribed by the Reserve Bank of India and applicable auditing standards. Candidates must ensure rigorous application of these statutory principles during banking and NBFC audit engagements.

questions.category: Asset Classification - Agricultural Advances
questions.question:
Kisan Vikas Bank granted direct agricultural loans to several farming societies. In assessing whether these accounts have turned into Non-Performing Assets (NPAs), which of the following criteria correctly reflects RBI directions?

Statement I: For short-duration crop loans, an account is classified as NPA if the installment of principal or interest thereon remains overdue for two crop seasons.
Statement II: For long-duration crop loans, an account is classified as NPA if the installment of principal or interest thereon remains overdue for one crop season.
Statement III: For agricultural loans not specified in the RBI circular (e.g., loans for setting up agro-processing units), identification of NPA is done on the same 90-day overdue basis as non-agricultural advances.
options: Statement I only
Statements I and II only
Statements II and III only
Statements I, II and III
questions.explanation: As per RBI prudential norms on agricultural advances: (i) Direct agricultural advances listed in the circular are assessed based on crop seasons: a loan granted for short-duration crops will be treated as NPA if the installment of principal or interest thereon remains overdue for two crop seasons; (ii) A loan granted for long-duration crops will be treated as NPA if overdue for one crop season; and (iii) For agricultural loans not specified in the circular, identification of NPA is done on the same basis as non-agricultural advances (i.e., 90 days overdue). All three statements are correct. Therefore, this treatment strictly aligns with the regulatory framework prescribed by the Reserve Bank of India and applicable auditing standards. Candidates must ensure rigorous application of these statutory principles during banking and NBFC audit engagements.

questions.category: Restructured Advances
questions.question:
Which of the following statements is INCORRECT regarding the restructuring of advances by commercial banks as per RBI guidelines?

Statement 1: Restructuring is an act in which a lender grants concession to a borrower for reasons relating to the borrower's financial difficulty.
Statement 2: Restructuring may involve alteration of installment amount, repayment period, rate of interest, or sanction terms.
Statement 3: Banks are legally entitled to restructure advance accounts with retrospective effect if sanctioned by the Board of Directors.
Statement 4: On restructuring, an account classified as Standard will be immediately downgraded to Sub-standard, whereas existing NPAs will remain in their same classification category.
options: Statement 1
Statement 2
Statement 3
Statement 4
questions.explanation: As per RBI prudential guidelines: Banks can restructure accounts classified under any category (standard, sub-standard, or doubtful); however, banks CANNOT restructure accounts with retrospective effect. Therefore, Statement 3 is incorrect. Statements 1, 2, and 4 are completely accurate: restructuring grants concessions due to borrower financial difficulty, involves modification of terms, and results in standard accounts being downgraded to sub-standard, while existing NPAs retain their pre-restructuring classification category.

questions.category: Upgradation of NPA Accounts
questions.question:
During the verification of loan accounts upgraded from NPA to Standard category during the year, an auditor noticed that Account X was upgraded after the borrower deposited a token amount representing 20% of the overdue interest, leaving principal arrears uncleared. Account Y was upgraded on March 31, 2024 based on a cheque received on April 5, 2024 (post-cut-off date).

In accordance with bank audit guidelines on upgradation of accounts, what should the auditor conclude?
options: Both upgradations are fully valid because partial recovery demonstrates revived creditworthiness and subsequent recoveries relate back to balance sheet date.

Both upgradations are improper: an NPA account can be upgraded to Standard only if the entire arrears of interest and principal are wiped out completely by genuine recoveries, and recoveries made after the balance sheet cut-off date cannot be used to upgrade the account as of the balance sheet date.
Account X is validly upgraded under the partial recovery doctrine, but Account Y is invalid.
Account Y is validly upgraded under SA 560 subsequent events rules, but Account X is invalid.
questions.explanation: Under RBI guidelines and bank audit procedures, an account classified as NPA can be upgraded to the Standard category ONLY if the overdue portion (entire arrears of interest and principal) is wiped out completely through genuine recoveries. Auditors must be vigilant against incorrect upgradation based on partial recoveries where arrears persist. Furthermore, recoveries made after the cut-off date cannot be backdated to upgrade the account as on the balance sheet date. Both Account X and Account Y were improperly upgraded.

questions.category: Sale/Purchase of NPAs
questions.question:
A commercial bank is considering the sale and purchase of non-performing assets (NPAs) to manage its balance sheet stress. Which of the following conditions is MANDATORY for the sale or purchase of NPAs between banks under RBI directions?

1. Only such NPAs can be sold which have remained as NPA in the books of the selling bank for at least 2 years.
2. NPAs must be sold/purchased 'without recourse' only, transferring the entire credit risk to the purchasing bank on cash basis.
3. If an NPA is sold below its Net Book Value (NBV), the shortfall must be debited to Profit & Loss Account; if sold for more than NBV, the excess must be utilized to meet loss on sale of other NPAs.
4. A bank is permitted to repurchase an NPA which it had originally sold after a cooling period of 12 months.
options: 1, 2 and 3 only
2, 3 and 4 only
1 and 2 only
questions.explanation: Under RBI directions for sale/purchase of NPAs: (i) Only such NPA can be sold which remained NPA in books for at least 2 years; (ii) NPA must be sold/purchased 'without recourse' only (entire credit risk transferred), on a cash basis only; (iii) Subsequent to sale, the selling bank assumes no risk; (iv) A bank CANNOT purchase an NPA which it had originally sold (repurchase is strictly prohibited, making statement 4 false); (v) If sold below Net Book Value (NBV), the shortfall is debited to P&L; and (vi) If sold above NBV, the excess is utilized to meet loss on sale of other NPAs. This statutory directive ensures complete risk mitigation and strict transparency across the regulated financial sector. Consequently, the auditor must verify full adherence to these compliance parameters without exception.

questions.category: Sale/Purchase of NPAs
questions.question: Global Bank purchased a portfolio of NPAs from Horizon Bank for Rs. 40 crores (Net Book Value in Horizon Bank was Rs. 60 crores). In the subsequent year, Global Bank recovered Rs. 48 crores from the acquired assets. What is the correct accounting treatment for the recovery and the risk weight to be assigned for capital adequacy by Global Bank as the purchasing bank?
options: The initial Rs. 40 crores recovered is adjusted against the acquisition cost, the excess Rs. 8 crores is recognized as profit in P&L, and a 100% risk weight is assigned for capital adequacy.
The entire Rs. 48 crores must be recognized as fee income, and a 0% risk weight is assigned because the assets were purchased at a discount.
The excess Rs. 8 crores must be credited directly to Capital Reserve, and a 150% risk weight is assigned as consumer exposure.
No profit can be recognized until all purchased assets are fully liquidated, and risk weight is determined by external credit rating agencies.
questions.explanation: As per RBI guidelines for purchased NPAs: (i) Any recovery from an NPA purchased is first adjusted against its acquisition cost (Rs. 40 crores), and any excess recovered (Rs. 8 crores) is recognized as profit in the Profit and Loss Account; (ii) In the books of the purchasing bank, provision must be made for the NPA purchased as per its classification status in the purchasing bank's books; and (iii) For capital adequacy purposes, banks must assign a 100% risk weight to NPAs purchased from other banks.

questions.category: Verification of Assets - Cash and ATM/CDM Balances
questions.question:
Case Scenario 5:
During the statutory audit of Pragyan Commercial Bank Ltd. for the financial year ended March 31, 2024, the audit team undertook the verification of several asset classes across corporate and branch operations:
1. Cash and Currency: Cash balances across physical branches, foreign currencies held at forex branches, automated teller machines (ATMs), and cash deposit machines (CDMs) were scheduled for physical verification. The branch manager argued that cash in off-site ATMs and CDMs need not be physically verified by statutory auditors as daily digital dispenser logs are generated.
2. Balances with RBI and Other Banks: In the bank reconciliation statements (BRS) with other banks, the audit team noticed several items: (a) Cash transactions remaining unresponded for 8 days, (b) Other debit and credit entries remaining unresponded for over 25 days, (c) Revenue items requiring write-offs/adjustments, and (d) Foreign currency balances held with overseas correspondent banks which the bank converted into INR using the average exchange rate of the financial year.
3. Money at Call and Short Notice: The bank lent Rs. 150 crores at call to other banks and borrowed Rs. 120 crores at short notice from financial institutions. In the balance sheet, management presented a net asset figure of Rs. 30 crores under 'Money at Call and Short Notice'.
4. Non-Banking Assets Acquired in Satisfaction of Claims (NBA): The bank acquired an industrial property with an outstanding advance of Rs. 12 crores; the net realizable value (NRV) was appraised at Rs. 9 crores. The bank recorded the property at Rs. 12 crores. Additionally, the bank held an immovable commercial property acquired 9 years ago in satisfaction of a claim, which was neither used for the bank's own business nor disposed of.

Evaluate the branch manager's contention regarding physical verification of cash held at ATMs and CDMs by statutory auditors:
options: The branch manager's contention is valid because electronic logs in CBS provide conclusive audit evidence of physical existence.

The branch manager's contention is incorrect; statutory audit procedures mandate carrying out physical verification of cash, including foreign currency, cash at ATMs, and cash deposit machines (CDMs) near the balance sheet date.
Physical verification is mandatory only for base branch vaults; off-site ATMs are audited exclusively by internal security personnel.
Physical verification of ATM cash is required once every three years by statutory central auditors only.
questions.explanation: As per the audit procedures for verification of cash in banks, the auditor must carry out physical verification of cash (including foreign currency, cash at ATMs, and cash deposit machines) near the balance sheet date. Electronic logs or digital dispenser reports cannot substitute for physical verification of cash balances. The auditor must satisfy themselves regarding the existence and physical possession of cash across all holding points, including ATMs and CDMs.

questions.explanation: For Non-Banking Assets Acquired in Satisfaction of Claims (NBA): (i) The asset must be recorded at lower of net book value of advance or net realizable value (NRV) of the asset (hence Rs. 9 crores, not Rs. 12 crores); (ii) The auditor must verify ownership is legally vested in the bank and held with intention of disposal; and (iii) Under Section 9 of the Banking Regulation Act, 1949, a bank is strictly restricted from holding any immovable property for a period exceeding 7 years from the date of acquisition, unless such property is required for the bank's own use.

questions.category: Verification of Investments - Portfolio Review and Shifting
questions.question:
Case Scenario 6:
During the audit of investments at Aryavart Bank, the statutory central auditors examined the investment portfolio consisting of Central and State Government securities, bonds of public sector undertakings, and equity shares. The bank also operated an active Portfolio Management Scheme (PMS) for high-net-worth clients.
1. Classification and Review: The investment portfolio was categorized into Held to Maturity (HTM), Available for Sale (AFS), and Held for Trading (HFT). The bank undertook an annual review of the investment portfolio on March 31, 2024. During the year, the treasury team shifted securities from AFS to HTM upon verbal approval from the Chief Investment Officer.
2. Portfolio Management Services (PMS): Aryavart Bank maintained PMS investments integrated within its general investment portfolio without conducting an independent audit of PMS operations, contending that statutory central audit of the bank covers all investment operations.
3. Physical Verification & Bank Receipts (BRs): Several Bank Receipts (BRs) for government securities purchases had been outstanding for more than 45 days, for which no written explanation was obtained by the internal inspection team.

With respect to the frequency of investment portfolio reviews and the procedure for shifting securities between categories (AFS to HTM), what are the mandatory requirements?
options: Banks are required to undertake quarterly reviews of their investment portfolio, and shifting from AFS to HTM requires approval from the RBI Governor.

Banks should undertake half-yearly reviews (as of 30th September and 31st March) of their investment portfolio; entire investments are classified under 3 categories (HTM, HFT & AFS); and shifting of investment from AFS to HTM must be duly approved by the Board of Directors (BOD).
Investment reviews are mandated only annually on March 31st, and category shifting is delegated entirely to the treasury head.
Shifting between investment categories is strictly prohibited under RBI Master Directions under any circumstances.
questions.explanation: As per the guidelines for verification of investments in banks: (i) Banks should undertake half-yearly reviews (as of 30th September and 31st March) of their investment portfolio; (ii) Entire investments of a bank are classified under 3 categories: Held to Maturity (HTM), Held for Trading (HFT), and Available for Sale (AFS); and (iii) Shifting of investments from AFS to HTM must be duly approved by the Board of Directors (BOD). Aryavart Bank failed by conducting only an annual review and shifting without Board approval. Therefore, this treatment strictly aligns with the regulatory framework prescribed by the Reserve Bank of India and applicable auditing standards. Candidates must ensure rigorous application of these statutory principles during banking and NBFC audit engagements.

questions.category: Verification of Capital - CRAR & Tier Capital
questions.question:
Case Scenario 7:
During the audit of Capital and Liabilities of Utkarsh Bank Ltd. as on March 31, 2024, the engagement team noted the following aspects:
1. Capital Adequacy: The bank reported a Capital to Risk-weighted Assets Ratio (CRAR) of 8.4%. Tier I capital comprised share capital and disclosed reserves, while Tier II capital included revaluation reserves and subordinated debt. Management claimed that an 8.4% CRAR is satisfactory as it exceeds 8%.
2. Borrowings and Bills Payable: The bank rediscounted commercial bills of Rs. 40 crores and obtained refinance of Rs. 60 crores from SIDBI, clubbing both together as 'Rediscount from Financial Institutions'. Under bills payable, the bank had issued demand drafts on plain paper printouts without printed serial numbers, and private secret codes were accessible to all clerical staff.
3. CASA and Term Deposits: The branch had several deposit accounts: (a) Savings accounts with no transactions for over 2 years were operated by teller staff without special revival verification; (b) Bulk term deposits of Rs. 3 crores were accepted at negotiated preferential interest rates without Board authorization; (c) Interest accrued but not due of Rs. 14 lakhs on term deposits was added directly to the principal balance of Term Deposits in the balance sheet; and (d) Foreign currency deposits of USD 5,00,000 were paid interest calculated on the basis of 365 days in a year.

With respect to Utkarsh Bank Ltd.'s Capital Risk Adequacy Ratio (CRAR) and capital tiers, evaluate the correctness of the regulatory position:
options: The bank's CRAR of 8.4% is adequate because Basel III minimum requirement is 8.0%.

The bank's CRAR is deficient because RBI requires banks to maintain a minimum CRAR of 9%; Tier I capital consists mainly of share capital and disclosed reserves (highest quality, fully available to cover losses), whereas Tier II capital has lower loss absorption capacity.
RBI mandates a minimum CRAR of 12% for all commercial banks regardless of asset size.
Tier II capital is superior in loss absorption to Tier I capital because subordinated debt holders have no voting rights.
questions.explanation: As per RBI prudential norms, RBI requires banks to maintain a minimum Capital to Risk-weighted Assets Ratio (CRAR) of 9% (calculated as Eligible Total Capital Funds / Risk weighted assets & off-balance sheet items * 100). Capital is divided into Tier I (highest quality capital, consisting mainly of share capital and disclosed reserves, fully available to cover losses) and Tier II (reserves and subordinated debt, having lower loss absorption capacity). Utkarsh Bank's CRAR of 8.4% fails to meet the mandatory 9% regulatory threshold.

Regarding Borrowings and Bills Payable internal controls, which of the following evaluations correctly reflects the audit requirements?
options: A clear distinction must be made between 'rediscount' and 'refinance' under borrowings; and controls over bills payable require that drafts/mail transfers be made on standard printed forms, unused forms kept under custody of a responsible officer, and the bank have a reliable private code known only to responsible officers.

Evaluate the audit procedures and regulatory rules governing CASA and Term Deposits observed in Utkarsh Bank Ltd.:

1. A current or savings account is treated as inoperative if there are no transactions for two years, and the auditor must verify revived/closed accounts on a sample basis.
2. Bulk deposits for scheduled commercial banks are presently defined as single deposits of Rs. 2 crore and above, where correct interest rates must be verified.

Which of the above statements are correct?
options: 1 and 2 only
1, 2 and 3 only
2, 3 and 4 only
questions.explanation: All four statements represent established audit and regulatory rules for bank deposits: (i) Current/savings accounts are treated as inoperative if there are no transactions for 2 years; (ii) Bulk deposits are single term deposits of Rs. 2 crore and above for scheduled commercial banks; (iii) Interest accrued but not due on deposits must be shown under 'Other Liabilities and Provisions' and NOT added to the deposits balance; and (iv) On premature closure of term deposits, deduction of foreclosure penalty must be verified. In respect of Deposits Designated in Foreign Currencies, which of the following represents the correct audit and accounting requirements?

Statement I: Foreign currency deposits must be converted into Indian Rupees at the rate notified by the bank's head office.
Statement II: Any resultant increase or decrease upon conversion must be taken to the Profit and Loss Account.
Statement III: Interest on foreign currency deposits must be paid on the basis of 360 days in a year.

Statements II and III only
Statements I and III only

Utkarsh Bank's calculation of interest on a 365-day basis was incorrect. All three statements are correct.

questions.category: Verification of Contingent Liabilities - Disclosure Requirements
questions.question:
Case Scenario 8:
During the audit of Contingent Liabilities of Navodaya Bank Ltd. for the year ended March 31, 2024, the statutory auditors examined the off-balance sheet disclosures and related internal controls:
1. Disclosures: The bank disclosed the following items under Contingent Liabilities: (a) Claims against the bank not acknowledged as debts, (b) Liability for partly paid investments, (c) Outstanding forward exchange and derivative contracts, (d) Guarantees given on behalf of constituents in India and outside India, and (e) Acceptances, endorsements and other obligations.
2. Crystallised Claim: An ongoing taxation dispute of Rs. 8 crores was decided against the bank by the Supreme Court on March 25, 2024, creating an undisputed liability to pay. The bank included this Rs. 8 crores under 'Claims against the bank not acknowledged as debts' within contingent liabilities, arguing that formal payment notice from the tax authority had not been received.
3. Management Representation: The bank management declined to provide a representation letter regarding off-balance sheet transactions, stating that external confirmations from guarantee beneficiaries are sufficient.

Which of the following items is NOT an off-balance sheet contingent liability required to be disclosed by a bank as per the prescribed format of balance sheet (Third Schedule)?

1. Claims against the bank not acknowledged as debts
2. Liability for partly paid investments
3. Overdue installments of principal and interest on non-performing loans
4. Guarantees given on behalf of constituents in India and outside India, and acceptances, endorsements and other obligations
options: 1 only
2 only
3 only
4 only
questions.explanation: The disclosure requirements of contingent liabilities for banks under the Third Schedule include: (i) Claims against the bank not acknowledged as debts; (ii) Liability for partly paid investments; (iii) Liability of outstanding forward exchange contracts & derivative contracts; (iv) Guarantees given on behalf of constituents in India or outside India; (v) Acceptances, endorsements and other obligations; and (vi) Other items for which the bank is contingently liable. Overdue installments on loans (item 3) are funded on-balance sheet advances and are accounted for under Advances (with provisioning), not contingent liabilities. Therefore, this treatment strictly aligns with the regulatory framework prescribed by the Reserve Bank of India and applicable auditing standards. Candidates must ensure rigorous application of these statutory principles during banking and NBFC audit engagements.

questions.category: Verification of Contingent Liabilities - Crystallised Liabilities & Management Representation

3. Management Representation: The bank management declined to provide a representation letter regarding off-balance sheet transactions, stating that external confirmations from guarantee beneficiaries are sufficient.

Evaluate the bank's treatment of the Rs. 8 crore Supreme Court tax liability and the management representation requirements for contingent liabilities:
options: The Rs. 8 crore item is properly disclosed as a contingent liability until demand notice is received, and management representations are optional.

The Rs. 8 crore tax dispute has crystallized into a definite liability upon the Supreme Court ruling and requires creation of a provision in the financial statements; it cannot be retained as a contingent liability. Furthermore, the auditor must obtain a written management representation confirming that disclosed contingent liabilities do not include any crystallized liabilities requiring provision.
Crystallized liabilities should be disclosed in the Directors' Report rather than provided in the Profit & Loss Account.
The auditor must issue an adverse opinion immediately without requesting management to create a provision.
questions.explanation: Auditors must obtain a management representation stating that: (i) All off-balance sheet transactions are accounted when they take place, (ii) Entered after following due procedure, (iii) Supported by underlying documents, (iv) All year-end contingent liabilities have been disclosed, and (v) Disclosed contingent liabilities DO NOT include any crystallised liabilities which require creation of provision in FS. Since the Supreme Court ruled against the bank on March 25, 2024, the tax liability of Rs. 8 crores has crystallised into a present obligation requiring a provision in the financial statements under AS 29 / principles of accounting. Disclosing it as a contingent liability is incorrect.

questions.category: Auditor's Report - Reporting to Central Government in Nationalised Banks
questions.question:
Case Scenario 9:
M/s R. Gupta & Associates was appointed as the statutory central auditor of Rashtriya Bank (a Nationalised Bank) and M/s T. Shah & Co. was appointed as the statutory auditor of Vikas Commercial Bank Ltd. (a Banking Company incorporated under the Companies Act, 2013). During the course of reporting for the financial year ended March 31, 2024, the following situations arose:
1. Nationalised Bank Reporting: M/s R. Gupta & Associates prepared their audit report for Rashtriya Bank addressed to the Central Government. The report omitted to state whether transactions coming to the auditor's notice were within the powers of the bank and whether returns from branches were adequate.
2. Banking Company Reporting: Vikas Commercial Bank Ltd. prepared its financial statements. The management insisted that CARO, 2020 is applicable to banking companies. M/s T. Shah & Co. evaluated reporting on Section 143(3) matters, including pending litigations, foreseeable losses, IEPF transfers, dividend compliance, and audit trail.
3. Long Form Audit Report (LFAR): The statutory branch auditors submitted their LFAR questionnaire to the statutory central auditors. The central auditors consolidated the LFAR and submitted it to the bank's management on June 15, 2024. The bank management submitted the LFAR together with the Board's views to the RBI on October 25, 2024 (132 days later).

In the case of a nationalised bank, which of the following matters is the statutory auditor MANDATED to state in the audit report to the Central Government?

1. Whether, in case the auditor had called for any explanation or information, it has been given.
2. Whether the balance sheet exhibits a true and fair view of the affairs of the bank.
3. Whether the profit and loss account shows a true balance of profit or loss for the period covered.
4. Whether transactions which have come to the auditor's notice are within the powers of the bank.
5. Whether returns received from branches have been found adequate for the audit.
6. Any other matter which the auditor considers should be brought to the notice of the Central Government.
options: 1, 2, 3 and 4 only
2, 3, 4 and 5 only
1, 4 and 6 only
questions.explanation: In the case of a nationalised bank, the auditor is required to report to the Central Government stating: (i) In case the auditor had called for any explanation or information, whether it has been given; (ii) Whether the balance sheet contains all necessary particulars and is properly drawn up so as to exhibit a true and fair view of affairs; (iii) Whether profit and loss account shows true balance of profit or loss; (iv) Whether transactions which have come to auditor's notice are within powers of the bank; (v) Whether returns received from branches of the bank have been found adequate for audit; and (vi) Any other matter which auditor considers to be brought to notice of Central Government. All six matters are mandatory. Therefore, this treatment strictly aligns with the regulatory framework prescribed by the Reserve Bank of India and applicable auditing standards. Candidates must ensure rigorous application of these statutory principles during banking and NBFC audit engagements.

Regarding the reporting obligations of M/s T. Shah & Co. for Vikas Commercial Bank Ltd. under the Companies Act, 2013 and CARO, 2020, which of the following statements is correct?

Besides the Independent Auditor's Report and LFAR, the statutory central auditor of a bank is required to issue various other reports and certificates. Which of the following is NOT an established report/certificate provided by the statutory central auditor?

1. Report on operating effectiveness of Internal Financial Controls over Financial Reporting (IFCoFR)
2. Report on serious irregularities under Section 143(12) of the Companies Act, 2013
3. Report on compliance with SLR requirements
4. Report on income recognition, asset classification and provisioning (IRACP)
5. Certificate on corporate governance
6. Certificate determining tax liabilities of individual loan customers of the bank

3 and 4 only
5 only
6 only
questions.explanation: Statutory central auditors provide reports and certificates on: (i) Operating effectiveness of Internal Financial Controls over Financial Reporting (IFCoFR); (ii) Report on any serious irregularity as per Section 143(12) of Companies Act, 2013; (iii) Long Form Audit Report (LFAR); (iv) Report on compliance with SLR requirements; (v) Report on income recognition, asset classification and provisioning (IRACP); and (vi) Certificate on corporate governance. Auditors do not certify the individual tax liabilities of a bank's borrowers (item 6), as that is outside the scope of bank audit. questions.category: Concurrent Audit - Meaning and Scope
questions.question:
Case Scenario 10:
Mahalakshmi Bank instituted a concurrent audit system across all its large and critical branches. During the review of the concurrent audit mechanism by the Audit Committee of the Board of Directors (ACB), the following matters were examined:
1. Nature and Scope: The Chief Internal Auditor explained that concurrent audit is a pre-audit where transactions are approved before execution. The scope of concurrent audit was determined independently by the Branch Managers of the respective branches without consulting the ACB.
2. Appointment and Tenure: CA Sandeep was appointed as external concurrent auditor for the Industrial Finance Branch in April 2019 and continued at the same branch continuously until March 2024 (5 continuous years). The ACB noted that while ACB decides maximum tenure up to 5 years, CA Sandeep argued that he could continue at the same branch for the entire 5 years.
3. Reporting and Frauds: During concurrent audit at the Overseas Branch, CA Sandeep discovered a fraudulent foreign exchange transaction of Rs. 45 lakhs involving forged letters of credit. CA Sandeep recorded the finding in his quarterly routine audit report to be submitted to the branch manager at the end of the quarter, without any immediate reporting.

Evaluate the Chief Internal Auditor's explanation regarding the nature and scope determination of concurrent audit:
options: The explanation is correct; concurrent audit is a pre-audit designed to grant prior approval to transactions.

The explanation is incorrect; concurrent audit is an audit or verification of transactions or activities concurrently as the transaction takes place (it is NOT a pre-audit; it is similar to internal audit to verify authenticity within the shortest possible time); and the detailed scope and coverage of branches must be determined by the Inspection & Audit Department with approval of the Audit Committee of the Board of Directors (ACB), not branch managers.
Scope is determined solely by the statutory central auditors during annual planning.
Concurrent audit is identical to external statutory audit and is governed exclusively by Section 143(8) branch audit rules.
questions.explanation: As defined in bank audit guidance: Concurrent audit is an audit or verification of transactions or activities of an organisation concurrently as the transaction/activity takes place. It is NOT a pre-audit. The concept is to verify authenticity of transactions/activities within the shortest possible time and is similar to internal audit. Furthermore, the detailed scope and coverage of branches is determined by the Inspection & Audit Department of the bank with the approval of the Audit Committee of Board of Directors (ACB).

questions.category: Concurrent Audit - Appointment and Tenure of External Auditors
questions.question:
Case Scenario 10:
Mahalakshmi Bank instituted a concurrent audit system across all its large and critical branches. During the review of the concurrent audit mechanism by the Audit Committee of the Board of Directors (ACB), the following matters were examined:
1. Nature and Scope: The Chief Internal Auditor explained that concurrent audit is a pre-audit where transactions are approved before execution. The scope of concurrent audit was determined independently by the Branch Managers of the respective branches without consulting the ACB.
2. Appointment and Tenure: CA Sandeep was appointed as external concurrent auditor for the Industrial Finance Branch in April 2019 and continued at the same branch continuously until March 2024 (5 continuous years). The ACB noted that while ACB decides maximum tenure up to 5 years, CA Sandeep argued that he could continue at the same branch for the entire 5 years.
3. Reporting and Frauds: During concurrent audit at the Overseas Branch, CA Sandeep discovered a fraudulent foreign exchange transaction of Rs. 45 lakhs involving forged letters of credit. CA Sandeep recorded the finding in his quarterly routine audit report to be submitted to the branch manager at the end of the quarter, without any immediate reporting.

With respect to the tenure of CA Sandeep as external concurrent auditor at the Industrial Finance Branch (5 continuous years at the same branch), what is the regulatory restriction?
options: CA Sandeep is fully entitled to continue at the same branch for 5 years because the overall maximum tenure determined by ACB is 5 years.

CA Sandeep's continuation at the same branch exceeds the statutory ceiling: although the ACB shall decide the maximum tenure of external concurrent auditors (generally not more than 5 years), NO concurrent auditor shall continue with a particular branch for more than 3 years.
Concurrent auditors must rotate annually across all branches without exception.
Tenure limits apply only to internal bank staff; external CA firms can continue indefinitely at a branch subject to annual renewal.
questions.explanation: Under RBI guidelines on concurrent audit: ACB of the bank shall decide the maximum tenure of external concurrent auditors, which generally shall not be more than 5 years. However, there is a specific restriction: 'no concurrent auditor shall continue with a branch for more than 3 years'. Therefore, retaining CA Sandeep at the Industrial Finance branch for 5 consecutive years directly breaches the 3-year single-branch tenure cap.

questions.question:

2. Critically evaluate CA Sandeep's action of including the fraudulent foreign exchange transaction of Rs. 45 lakhs in the routine quarterly report instead of immediate reporting:
options: CA Sandeep acted properly because concurrent auditors are only authorized to communicate through formal quarterly reports.

CA Sandeep's action is severely deficient: minor irregularities are to be rectified in a timely manner, but serious irregularities should be reported to the head office for immediate action; and if fraudulent transactions are detected, they must IMMEDIATELY be reported to the Inspection & Audit Department of the bank, the Chief Vigilance Officer (CVO), and concerned Branch Managers.
Fraudulent transactions should be reported directly to local police authorities, bypassing bank management entirely.

Deferring the reporting of a Rs. 45 lakh fraud to a routine quarterly report undermines fraud containment and violates reporting guidelines.

questions.category: Concurrent Audit - Focus Areas
questions.question:
In concurrent audit of banking operations, specific procedures must be performed in high-risk focus areas. Which of the following pairs of Focus Area and Audit Procedure is INCORRECTLY matched?

A. Advances - Ensure loans are sanctioned properly, securities received/registered, proper post-disbursement supervision, LCs within delegated power, BG register properly recorded, follow-up of overdue bills, and verify classification under RBI guidelines.
B. Foreign Exchange - Check inward/outward remittances properly accounted, examine extension/cancellation of forward contracts, ensure Nostro balances within limits, reconcile Nostro and Vostro accounts, and ensure adherence to dealing room guidelines.
C. Serious Irregularities by External Concurrent Auditors - If noticed, appointment may be cancelled and fact may be reported to RBI and ICAI.
D. Zone-wise Reporting - Concurrent audit findings must be reported zone-wise directly to the Comptroller and Auditor General (CAG) on a monthly basis.
options: A
B
C
D
questions.explanation: Statement D is incorrect because there should be zone-wise reporting of findings of concurrent audit to the Audit Committee of the Board of Directors (ACB), NOT to the CAG. Statements A, B, and C accurately state the focus areas for advances, foreign exchange transactions, and the action taken (reporting to RBI and ICAI) if serious irregularities are noticed in the working of external concurrent auditors. Therefore, this treatment strictly aligns with the regulatory framework prescribed by the Reserve Bank of India and applicable auditing standards. Candidates must ensure rigorous application of these statutory principles during banking and NBFC audit engagements.

questions.category: NBFC Definition & 50-50 Principle Test
questions.question:
Case Scenario 11:
FinTech Horizons Ltd. is an Indian company engaged in diverse financial and commercial activities. As of March 31, 2024, an analysis of its financial position and gross income revealed the following data:
- Total Assets (excluding intangible assets): Rs. 200 crores
- Financial Assets: Rs. 115 crores (57.5% of total assets)
- Gross Income: Rs. 30 crores
- Income from Financial Assets: Rs. 18 crores (60% of gross income)
- Net Owned Funds (NOF): Rs. 8 crores
FinTech Horizons Ltd. commenced business as an Investment and Credit Company (ICC) without obtaining a Certificate of Registration (CoR) from the RBI, arguing that since its Net Owned Funds are Rs. 8 crores, it is exempt from registration until NOF reaches Rs. 10 crores. Meanwhile, AltVenture Ltd. operates as a Venture Capital Fund registered with SEBI, and Apex Nidhi Ltd. operates as a Nidhi Company under Section 406 of Companies Act, 2013. The statutory auditor of AltVenture Ltd. and Apex Nidhi Ltd. questioned whether they must also register as NBFCs with the RBI.

Based on the '50-50 principle test' prescribed by the RBI, evaluate whether FinTech Horizons Ltd. qualifies as a Non-Banking Financial Company (NBFC):
options: FinTech Horizons Ltd. does not qualify as an NBFC because both financial assets and financial income must exceed 75% of total assets and gross income respectively.

FinTech Horizons Ltd. qualifies as an NBFC because its financial assets constitute more than 50% of total assets (excluding intangible assets) AND income from financial assets constitutes more than 50% of gross income (dual 50-50 criteria fulfilled).
FinTech Horizons Ltd. qualifies as an NBFC solely because its gross income exceeds Rs. 25 crores.
The 50-50 test is applicable only to deposit-taking companies; for non-deposit companies, asset size alone determines NBFC status.
questions.explanation: As per the RBI regulatory framework, a company will be treated as an NBFC when it satisfies the dual '50-50 test': (i) Financial assets constitute more than 50% of total assets (excluding intangible assets), and (ii) Income from financial assets constitutes more than 50% of gross income. A company fulfilling both these criteria qualifies as an NBFC and is required to be registered as an NBFC with the RBI. FinTech Horizons Ltd. has 57.5% financial assets and 60% financial income, thereby clearly meeting the 50-50 test.

FinTech Horizons Ltd. is an Indian company engaged in diverse financial and commercial activities. As of March 31, 2024, an analysis of its financial position and gross income revealed the following data:

FinTech Horizons Ltd. commenced business as an Investment and Credit Company (ICC) without obtaining a Certificate of Registration (CoR) from the RBI, arguing that since its Net Owned Funds are Rs. 8 crores, it is exempt from registration until NOF reaches Rs. 10 crores. Meanwhile, AltVenture Ltd. operates as a Venture Capital Fund registered with SEBI, and Apex Nidhi Ltd. operates as a Nidhi Company under Section 406 of Companies Act, 2013. The statutory auditor of AltVenture Ltd. and Apex Nidhi Ltd. questioned whether they must also register as NBFCs with the RBI.

Evaluate FinTech Horizons Ltd.'s legal position regarding commencement of NBFC business with Net Owned Funds of Rs. 8 crores without obtaining a CoR from RBI:
options: The company's action is valid because commencement of business is permissible while the CoR application is processed.

The company's action is illegal because no NBFC shall commence or carry on the business of an NBFC without: (i) obtaining a Certificate of Registration (CoR) issued by RBI, and (ii) having Net Owned Fund (NOF) of Rs. 10 crores (except Rs. 2 crores for NBFC-P2P, NBFC-AA, and NBFCs with no public funds, and Rs. 300 crores for NBFC-IFC and IDF-NBFC).
The minimum Net Owned Fund requirement for all NBFCs is Rs. 100 crores under the Scale Based Regulations.
An ICC is exempt from NOF requirements if it does not accept public deposits.
questions.explanation: Under Section 45-IA of the RBI Act, 1934, no NBFC shall commence or carry on the business of a non-banking financial institution without: (i) Obtaining a certificate of registration issued by RBI, and (ii) Having net owned fund of Rs. 10 crores (subject to Rs. 2 crores for NBFC-P2P, NBFC-AA, and NBFCs with no public funds, and Rs. 300 crores for NBFC-IFC and IDF-NBFC). FinTech Horizons Ltd. with NOF of Rs. 8 crores violates both conditions by carrying on ICC business without CoR and without meeting the Rs. 10 crore NOF threshold.
